power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p=0.95", Sentence = "The exception being slopes of the high classes in MCS and BiB where there was little statistical evidence that these differed; i.e., both are persistently high across time (p=0.95; Figure 1)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Background: Depression/anxiety symptoms emerge early in life.
We examined emotional symptom trajectories, from early childhood, in three UK birth-cohorts spanning successive generations and diverse socio-ethnic contexts.

We used data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), Millennium Cohort Study (MCS) and Born in Bradford (BiB) to identify groupbased emotional symptom trajectories from 3-14y (N=11,025; 15,446; 6,711).
Participants were born three decades apart (ALSPAC: 1990-2, MCS: 2000-2, BiB: 2007-10).
We characterised groups by: sex, ethnicity, maternal depression/anxiety and IMD quintile.
In ALSPAC we modelled associations between trajectories and depression/anxiety diagnoses at 24y and 30y.
Results: Participants from ethnic minority backgrounds comprised 4% of ALSPAC, 17% of MCS and 66% of BiB.
In all cohorts 49% were female.
Each cohort had low-, mid-and highlevel symptom trajectories.
High-level trajectories comprised 6-7% of children.
In younger cohorts (MCS and BiB), the high-level symptom trajectory started high and persisted while in the older ALSPAC cohort it started low and increased.
In MCS and BiB, low-to-medium-level symptoms increased over time, but remained stable in ALSPAC.
Female sex and maternal depression/anxiety were associated with increased odds of high-level trajectories (all cohorts).
Lower area-level deprivation and belonging to the local ethnic majority group were protective.
Mid-and high-level symptom trajectories had higher odds of depression/anxiety diagnoses in early adulthood in ALSPAC.
Conclusions: Childhood emotional symptom trajectory-groups are broadly similar across generations and diverse social contexts.
However, children born after 2000, in more diverse contexts, may experience persistent symptoms from a younger age.
Depression and anxiety symptoms often emerge early in life.
Approximately half of depression cases emerge before age 30 and nearly 40% of anxiety cases emerge before age 14 (Solmi et al., 2022).

text.text: However, studies investigating which sub-groups contribute to overall population level growth are lacking.
For example, we do not know whether the prevalence of children with persistent, high-level emotional symptoms has changed across generations.
Diverse, contemporary cohorts, using the same assessment method longitudinally are available but have so far been underutilised in comparative cross-cohort trajectory studies.

text.text: Studying long-term trends of early pre-clinical emotional symptoms is critical because clinical anxiety and depression often first manifest as emotional difficulties in childhood.

Capturing early onset and longitudinal trajectories can help inform strategies for prevention, intervention, and resource allocation involving health, education, social care and other agencies to improve long-term population-level outcomes.
Specifically, identifying groups of children with early-onset, persistent emotional problems in childhood through to adolescence.

Prior meta-analysis of longitudinal depressive symptom trajectories in childhood/adolescence shows that persistent emotional symptoms in early life predict later diagnoses of major depressive disorder (MDD) (Portogallo et al., 2024) alongside a range of poor social and physical health outcomes, for example NEET ("Not in education, employment or training") status (Morales-Muñoz et al., 2023; Rahmani & Groot, 2023).

text.text: In the current study we aimed to: a) identify a high/persistent emotional symptom trajectory group spanning early-childhood to early-adolescence in three generationally, ethnically, and socioeconomically diverse UK cohorts; b) compare group size/proportions, symptom severity over time and onset across cohorts; and c) characterise trajectory groups by sociodemographic factors, and their association with mental illness diagnosis in earlyadulthood.

text.text: We identified and characterised group-based early-childhood trajectories of emotional symptoms in three ethnically and socioeconomically diverse successive UK populationbased cohorts, born two decades apart.
Despite generational, ethnic and socioeconomic differences, we identified a high-level symptom group of a similar prevalence (6-7%) in all three cohorts.
Two key differences emerged.

In the high-level symptom trajectory, symptom level in childhood starts high and persists across time in the younger cohorts whereas in the oldest . cohort (born in the early 1990s) symptoms start low and steeply increase.

In the younger cohorts, born after 2000, mid-or low-level symptom trajectories show an increase in symptom level, and become closer to mid/high groups over time, unlike the oldest cohort (born early 1990s) where these groups are stable.
Considering both high-level and increasing symptom trajectories together, a larger proportion of children in the younger, more diverse cohorts belonged to these groups.
These findings support existing evidence that in recent decades emotional symptoms are increasing among children from an early age.
Particularly in groups that experience relatively low-level symptoms, while symptom severity in group of children experiencing high-level of symptoms remains stable.

Therefore, the overall picture is consistent with an increase in low-to-mid level symptoms in young children in recent decades, aligning with wider data trends in the UK showing a sharp rise in the incidence of depression and anxiety in young people from as young as six years old since 2012 (Cybulski et al., 2021).

text.text: Across all cohorts, female sex and maternal depression/anxiety were associated with higher odds of persistent or increasing symptom trajectories, whereas higher SES and belonging to the local ethnic majority were protective factors.
Prevalence of persistent-high symptoms aligns with broader trajectory literature despite differences in age, geography, and psychiatric measure.
Group-based trajectory modelling studies identified in a large systematic review (Shore et al., 2018) mostly studied US populations with trajectories starting later (in early/mid adolescence).

text.text: Our findings build upon these, suggesting that that overall population growth may be attributed to symptom increases in children with initially mild to moderate symptoms rather than increased prevalence of children experiencing persistently high emotional symptoms from an early age.

Like our findings, previously identified predictors of trajectories with greater symptom burden include female gender, maternal depression/anxiety, lower income/education and non-white ethnicity (Dachew et al., 2023; Shore et al., 2018; Tseliou et al., 2024).

text.text: However, research frequently excludes underrepresented populations and ethnic minority groups which are often at highest risk.
Our findings build on these by comparing findings in ALSPAC (a largely white, higher SES cohort) with trajectories in two more diverse UK cohorts (MCS and BiB).
In the BiB cohort, belonging to an ethnic minority group was associated with lower odds of persistent high symptoms which contrasts with findings in other cohorts.
Bradford, where the BiB cohort is based, has a large community of South Asian heritage.

Previous findings in the cohort show South Asian mothers had a lower incidence of common mental health disorders compared to white mothers (Santorelli et al., 2024), our results are consistent with these findings.

However, this observation might also be explained by underreporting of mental health problems in South Asian communities.
Generational differences in social determinants of emotional problems between the cohorts may underpin some of our findings.

Several of these factors disproportionately affect children of lower SES leading to higher emotional problems in this group, which is supported by our findings.

text.text: Our findings reinforce the importance of sociodemographic and early life risk factors in predicting mental health trajectories.
The two younger cohorts included in this study were more deprived overall which could explain the earlier onset and the higher proportion belonging to persistent/increasing trajectories.

Furthermore, rates of maternal depression/anxiety were higher in the youngest cohort and in MCS rates of severe maternal depression/anxiety were comparable to rates of all/any maternal depression/anxiety in ALSPAC.

Family psychiatric history and sociodemographic factors were common features in models identified by a recent systematic review of prediction models for anxiety/depression trajectories (Fairweather et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Family psychiatric history and sociodemographic factors were common features in models identified by a recent systematic review of prediction models for anxiety/depression trajectories <ref type="bibr">(Fairweather et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Increased mental health awareness and reduced stigma might partially explain increases in mild sub-clinical emotional symptoms.
In the current study we see a fairly stable proportion of young people belonging to a high-risk, persistent group while the proportion in low/mid symptom groups increase.
It has been suggested that reduced stigma and increased reporting/awareness of mental health in both young people and the parents of young people is contributing to this trend.

Although beneficial, an unintended consequence of reduced stigma and improved awareness of mental health might be wider recognition/reporting of subclinical or transient emotional symptoms that are overinterpreted as clinical anxiety or depression.

While this may lead to artefactual increases it has been hypothesised that this might drive genuine increases in new cases and worsening of existing cases by perpetuating behaviours such as avoidance (Foulkes & Andrews, 2023).

text.text: In the wider literature there is evidence of increasing severe CMD cases and symptoms (e.g., self-harm) in young people in the UK (Cybulski et al., 2021) as well as milder/moderate self-reported psychological distress.

text.text: Identifying increasing and persistent emotional trajectories, early, before symptoms escalate is a useful and novel way to differentiate this . group from children with mild transient symptoms; as highlighted in a recent Lancet Psychiatry Commission on youth mental health (McGorry et al., 2024).

text.text: A major strength of our study is replication of findings across three ethnically and socioeconomically diverse populations, including groups frequently underrepresented in mental health research and using a contemporary cohort.
We harmonized our modelling approaches across cohorts as far as possible.
However, analyses exploring associations between key demographic factors and the persistent trajectory group in the BiB cohort were likely underpowered.
Measurement invariance may explain the apparent increase in lowlevel symptoms, reflecting parent/teacher under-reporting earlier and more accurate selfreport later.
However, we conducted sensitivity analyses to test this possibility.
Broadly trajectory groups were unchanged which was reassuring.

The fact that both sex and maternal depression/anxiety associated with high-level vs low-level symptom trajectories in BiB (like the other cohorts) further supports the characterisation of these groups.
High symptom trajectory membership predicted depression/GAD diagnoses in early adulthood (in ALSPAC), strengthening the validity of our trajectory groupings.

Anxiety is often under researched compared to depression and our results support further research in this area as we high emotional symptom trajectories in early childhood strongly associates with future GAD diagnoses at age 24 and 30 in ALSPAC.
However, we found no evidence that high symptom trajectories predicted depression at age 30.

Given the finding at age 24 and strong existing evidence that childhood/adolescent symptoms persist into adulthood (Portogallo et al., 2024), it is likely that this finding reflects selection bias; attrition is a common limitation of longitudinal cohort data and there were substantially fewer depression cases in the high-persistent group at age 30.

text.text: In young, contemporary cohorts symptoms are emerging early.
Health, education, social care and other services need to be responsive to this emerging trend, which may have longterm implications for young people.
Early prediction of children at high-risk of developing persistent symptoms is an opportunity for early intervention and possible improvement of . long-term outcomes.
This would support better allocation of resources to children with the highest need.
However, ethical implications and risks of early screening for emotional symptoms in young people need consideration.
Future research also needs to explore individual causal predictors of early-emerging, persistent trajectories, across diverse groups and generations to understand drivers of early onset.
Our findings show that the prevalence of high-level emotional symptoms in early life remains stable across UK cohorts spanning different generations and diverse ethnic and socioeconomic contexts.
However, children in more diverse, contemporary cohorts appear more likely to experience persistently high symptom levels and increases from initially lower symptom trajectories.
These findings align with wider data trends in the UK showing a rise in the incidence of depression and anxiety in young people, along with earlier onset in younger generations.
Health, education, social care and other services need to be responsive to this emerging trend, which may have important long-term implications for young people.
